prompt.context: Six months out of HBS, a frustrated classmate calls you to complain that the fast food burger joint that he bought has been steadily losing money for the last 3 months. He wants to know what you think he should do about it.
prompt.question: Where do you start? What would you do to diagnose and address the problem?

clarifying_info.q: What do you mean by losing money — have profits declined or is the business in the red?
Have revenues decreased, costs increased, or both?
Are there fewer customers or are customers spending less per visit?
Is the revenue decline due to internal or external factors?
clarifying_info.a: The issue is external — a new competitor opened across the street three months ago.

clarifying_info.q: What does the new competitor offer?
clarifying_info.a: They serve chicken dinners and appear to offer a completely different experience.

framework: 1. Clarify the problem: define 'losing money' (profit decline vs. cash negative) and establish the baseline from 3+ months ago
2. Revenue vs. cost diagnosis: determine whether the issue is on the revenue side (fewer customers or lower spend per visit) or cost side

3. External vs. internal drivers of revenue decline: check for new competition, change in eating habits, local economic changes (business closings) vs. internal issues (food quality, prices, health code violations)
4. Competitive analysis: understand the new competitor's value proposition — food type, quality, price, service, facility, parking, access
5. Customer research: primary interviews at both locations to assess perception gaps and identify which burger customers have switched
6. Option generation and prioritization: develop menu, facility, quality, or marketing improvements; rank by traffic impact and ROI
7. Action plan: sequence initiatives with timing and ownership

questions.prompt: The business has been losing money for 3 months. Walk me through how you would diagnose the root cause.
questions.guidance: A strong answer starts by clarifying 'losing money', then builds a structured top-down tree: Revenue vs. Cost → if Revenue, then Volume vs. Price/mix → if Volume, then External vs. Internal drivers. Candidate should articulate each branch before asking for data, not jump straight to a hypothesis.

questions.prompt: You've established that the revenue decline is driven by fewer customers due to a new chicken restaurant across the street. How would you assess the competitive threat?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers: (1) first-hand visit — food quality, price, variety, service, cleanliness, facility layout, parking/access; (2) competitive benchmarking against the burger joint on the same dimensions; (3) primary customer research — interviews and paid taste tests at both locations; (4) segmenting former burger customers into switchers, dual-visitors, and net-new chicken customers.

questions.prompt: Based on your competitive assessment, how would you decide what actions to take?
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate a range of options (new menu items, improved quality, facility upgrades, pricing adjustments, marketing/promotions) and apply criteria to prioritize: speed of traffic recovery and return on investment. Should conclude with a structured action plan including timing and responsibilities. Bonus: acknowledge the option to evaluate whether to close/exit the facility if the economics are irreversible.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the possible reasons a fast food burger restaurant might be losing customers?

categories.name: External — competitive
ideas: Competitor offering higher quality or fresher ingredients
Competitor with more varied or healthier menu
Competitor with better facility, more seating, or easier parking

categories.name: External — market/environmental
ideas: Shift in consumer eating habits away from burgers
Local major employer closed, reducing foot traffic
Negative media coverage of the fast food category

categories.name: Internal — product & quality
ideas: Decline in food quality or consistency
Higher prices not justified by quality

categories.name: Internal — operations & service
ideas: Health code violation or food safety incident

categories.name: Internal — marketing & visibility
ideas: Poor signage or visibility from street

recommendation: Conduct an immediate competitive assessment of the new chicken restaurant through direct visits and customer interviews to identify the specific value gaps driving customer attrition
Prioritize 2-3 high-impact, fast-turnaround initiatives (e.g., menu addition, pricing adjustment, service improvement) based on customer feedback and ROI analysis
Develop a sequenced action plan with clear owners and timelines; reassess financials after 60-90 days to determine whether the business is viable long-term
risks: Improvement initiatives may require capital investment that the owner cannot fund
Customer habits may be permanently changed, limiting recovery potential
Competing on a different food category (chicken) may dilute the burger brand identity
next_steps: Visit the chicken restaurant and conduct a structured benchmarking exercise
Run 10-15 customer intercept interviews at both locations within two weeks
Model the unit economics of 2-3 improvement scenarios before committing capital
